---
title: "Quiz: histograms and a global threshold"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Object pixels are those with $I(x) > t$; $p_i$ is the normalised histogram and $P(t)$ the cumulative histogram.

---

**Q1.** An image has $N = 10\,000$ pixels, and 400 of them have grey level 200. What is $p_{200}$? What does it mean in words?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Divide by the number of pixels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$p_{200} = 400/10\,000 = 0.04$: a pixel chosen at random has grey level 200 with probability 4 %.
:::

---

**Q2.** $P(120) = 0.85$. Which fraction of the image does the threshold $t = 120$ call object?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$P(t)$ counts the pixels at or below $t$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1 - P(120) = 0.15$: 15 % of the pixels are brighter than 120 and become object.
:::

---

**Q3.** Two images have exactly the same histogram. Must a histogram-based threshold give masks of the same shape? Of the same area?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a histogram remember about the pixels?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Same area, yes: the threshold is the same and the area is $1 - P(t)$. Same shape, no: the histogram forgets where the pixels are, so one image may contain round blobs and the other scattered noise with the same grey levels.
:::

---

**Q4.** The valley of a histogram is deep and wide between 90 and 140. Why does it hardly matter where in the valley you put $t$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
When $t$ moves up by one grey level, which pixels change label?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only the pixels with grey level exactly at the threshold change label, and in a deep valley there are almost none. The mask (and its area) stays nearly the same for every $t$ in the valley.
:::

---

**Q5.** You add noise to a bimodal image. What happens to the two peaks and the valley, and what does the mask look like?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each pixel moves up or down by a random amount.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both peaks get wider, overlap, and the valley fills up. Pixels whose noise pushes them across $t$ are misclassified one by one: isolated wrong pixels (salt and pepper) in the object and in the background.
:::

---

**Q6.** A $5 \times 5$ mean filter is applied before thresholding. By which factor does it reduce the noise, and what is the price?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
An average of $n$ independent values.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It averages 25 pixels, so the noise standard deviation drops by $\sqrt{25} = 5$. The price: edges are blurred over about 5 pixels, so boundary pixels become mixtures (partial volume), small objects lose contrast, and the boundary of the mask is less precise.
:::

---

**Q7.** A 16-bit image from a 12-bit camera uses grey levels 100–3900. Why is a histogram with 256 bins over 0–65 535 a poor choice?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compute the bin width.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each bin is 256 grey levels wide, so all the data fall into about 15 bins: the peaks merge and the valley is invisible. Use bins over the range of the data (e.g. 256 bins over 100–3900) or one bin per grey level.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the mean grey level of the image equals $\sum_i i\, p_i$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Group the pixels by grey level.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\frac1N \sum_{\text{pixels } x} I(x) = \frac1N \sum_i i \cdot h_i = \sum_i i\,\frac{h_i}{N} = \sum_i i\,p_i$: summing over pixels is the same as summing over grey levels, each counted $h_i$ times.
:::
